32 CFR 117.3(b) defines ACCM verbatim: 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.' ACCM is thus a SAP-like access control that by definition sits outside the SAP reporting statutes.

32 CFR 117.23(d)(1): 'DoD SAP contracts. Contractors will implement the security requirements for SAPs codified in SAP-related policy, when established by contract. These documents include, but are not limited to, statutes, E.O.s, CSA directives, instructions, manuals, regulations, standards, memorandums, and other SAP security related policy documents.'

claims.text: The rule's source line is '85 FR 83312, Dec. 21, 2020', which dates the codified carve-out provision to the December 2020 NISPOM rulemaking.

32 CFR 117.3(b) defines SAP verbatim: 'SAP means any program that is established to control access and distribution and to provide protection for particularly sensitive classified information beyond that normally required for TOP SECRET, SECRET, or CONFIDENTIAL information.'

The carve-out is therefore not a classification device but an INSPECTION device: it removes the one federal agency that would otherwise physically visit, inspect, and record a cleared contractor facility performing the classified work. Nothing else in Part 117 substitutes an alternative external inspector; oversight reverts inside the SAP's own chain.

THE CONTRACTOR CARVE-OUT, in regulation. 32 CFR 117.6(b) (responsibilities of the Director, DCSA) verbatim: 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, "DoD SAP Policy".' The preceding sentence establishes what is being relieved: DCSA 'Provides security oversight of the NISP as the DoD CSO on behalf of DoD components and those non-DoD executive branch agencies who enter into agreements with DoD.'

Because 117.23(d)(1) exports the substantive SAP security requirements into contract documents, the actual rules governing a contractor holding SAP material are not published anywhere in the Code of Federal Regulations and are not obtainable without the contract. Reasoning: the regulation defers to unspecified 'SAP security related policy documents' established by contract.

32 CFR 117.23 addresses ACCM in the same supplement as SAPs, SCI, RD, FRD, TFNI and NNPI, requiring contractors to implement ACCM protection requirements 'when established by contract'.

claims.sourceText: 32 CFR 117.3(b) read against 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3)
claims.text: Because ACCM is defined as the case where SAP controls are not required, an ACCM is outside the definition of 'special access program' in 10 U.S.C. 119 and 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(3), and therefore outside every SAP congressional reporting statute. Reasoning: all four reporting statutes are triggered by the term 'special access program', which ACCM expressly is not.

ACCM is the only member of that regulated set with no reporting statute attached: 10 U.S.C. 119, 50 U.S.C. 2426, 3348 and 3091a each key on the term 'special access program' or 'controlled access program', and the NISPOM rule's own definition places ACCM expressly 'where SAP controls are not required.' A capability protected by ACCM rather than SAP controls therefore triggers no congressional notice under any of the four statutes. Reasoning stated from the definition and the four statutes.

claims.sourceText: Reading of 10 U.S.C. 119(e), EO 13526 sec. 4.3(b)(3) and 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) together; all three texts read from primary sources on 22 August 2026
claims.text: Three separate instruments each narrow oversight of the same object, and none of them depends on the others. 10 U.S.C. 119(e) reduces the congressional readership of a waived SAP to twelve members. EO 13526 sec. 4.3(b)(3) can reduce ISOO's access to one person. 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3) relieves the Director, DCSA of NISP industrial-security oversight entirely on a carve-out. Congressional, executive and industrial-security oversight are narrowed by three different authorities, so closing any one of them would leave the other two intact.

claims.nodeLabel: Waived unacknowledged special access program (waived USAP)
claims.text: The combination that produces a genuinely invisible program is not one provision but three stacked: 119(e) removes the content from the written record; the sec. 1061 Pub. L. 114-328 sunset (eff. 31 Dec 2021) removed the annual census that would otherwise show a count; and the DoDD 5205.07 carve-out provision (see 32 CFR 117.6) removes DCSA from the contractor facility where the work is performed. Each layer is individually lawful and documented; the stack is what defeats discovery. Reasoning stated.
